title: Eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and characteristic polynomial
terms: eigenvalue; characteristic value; eigenvector; characteristic vector; characteristic polyno- mial; characteristic equation.

exposition.text:
For a square matrix A, a nonzero vector v satisfying Av = λv is an eigenvector with eigenvalue
λ. Eigenvalues solve det(A − λI) = 0. The monic convention χ (t) = det(tI − A) differs only by

Eigenvectors are never zero, although zero may be an eigenvalue; this occurs exactly when A is
singular. Eigenvalues may depend on the scalar field: a real rotation can have no real eigenvec-

tors but have complex ones. For an eigenpair, p(A)v = p(λ)v; if A is invertible, A v = λ v.
Only scalar multiples of the same eigenvector, not coordinatewise reciprocals, are relevant.
A real matrix of odd size has a real eigenvalue because its real characteristic polynomial has
odd degree. The statement about eigenvectors of p(A) is one-way: different eigenvalues of A
can merge under p, creating new eigenvectors of p(A). If every nonzero vector is an eigenvector
of A, comparing basis vectors and their sums forces A to be a scalar multiple of the identity.

question.text:
Which statement holds for every real 5 × 5 matrix?
(A) All five eigenvalues are real.
(B) At least one eigenvalue is real.
(C) Zero is an eigenvalue.
(D) Every eigenvalue is positive.
(E) No eigenvalue can be repeated.

solution.text:
The characteristic polynomial is a real polynomial of odd degree. Its values have opposite
signs for sufficiently large positive and negative arguments, so the intermediate value theo-
rem gives a real root. Nonreal roots can still occur in conjugate pairs; zero, positivity, and
distinctness are not forced.
